title: MediBook Course Reflection & Feedback
instructions: Reflective course evaluation and learning outcomes for the Advanced Backend Development curriculum.
q1: 1. Which topic in this course did you find most challenging, and why?
a1: Database transactions and atomicity were by far the most challenging topic for me. At first, it was difficult to fully grasp the high stakes involved in multi-step operations—especially in clinic booking and financial cancellation workflows where partial failures directly lead to double bookings, financial discrepancies, or orphan records. Understanding how to properly coordinate ACID guarantees, manage pooled connections without resource leaks, and handle rollbacks in asynchronous Node.js required a fundamental mindset shift. Learning how to properly isolate operations using pessimistic row-level locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) versus application-level checks was conceptually demanding, but mastering it revealed how critical atomicity is for real-world reliability.
q2: 2. Describe one concept you understood only after the practical assignments. What made it click?
a2: Caching and in-memory queue management with Redis only truly clicked for me during the hands-on practical assignments. In class lectures, caching sounded like an abstract speed optimization. However, during the practical activities, running repeated requests and benchmark tests made the stark difference between disk-bound MySQL queries and sub-millisecond Redis in-memory lookups undeniable. Measuring that latency drop made the value of caching tangible. Furthermore, building the background worker with atomic Redis commands like LMOVE, BRPOP, and LPUSH showed me that Redis is far more than a simple cache—it is a powerful message broker that safely prevents race conditions and queue dropouts.
q3: 3. How has your approach to designing databases or APIs changed since the start of the trimester?
a3: My approach has transformed from an ad-hoc, UI-first perspective into a disciplined, engineering-first architectural methodology. At the beginning of the trimester, I designed tables casually with loose relationships and relied heavily on application-level JavaScript to enforce business rules. Today, I approach database design with rigorous 3NF normalization, enforcing integrity at the database layer using CHECK constraints, strict foreign key ON DELETE RESTRICT cascades, and generated stored columns with unique indexes (such as active_slot to safely permit rebooking cancelled slots). On the API side, I now design strictly according to RESTful conventions using plural resource nouns, proper HTTP verbs, and meaningful semantic status codes (201, 400, 404, 409, 422). Crucially, I now push complex groupings and recursive CTEs directly into SQL rather than wrangling data in memory in Node.js.
q4: 4. What would you improve about how this course was taught or assessed?
a4: The course was taught exceptionally well, with rigorous, authentic assessments that mirrored real-world software engineering demands. The teaching quality was 100% sound, and the foundational concepts were clearly explained and absorbed. The only enhancement I would recommend for future cohorts is extending the timeline of the summative project across a larger portion of the trimester. Providing more time would allow facilitators to conduct deeper individual follow-ups and 1-on-1 code reviews with each student to verify comprehensive mastery, as well as give learners more room to explore advanced distributed systems topics and deployment pipelines without the time crunch of an intensive deadline.
q5: 5. How do you plan to apply what you learned in this course going forward?
a5: I have already started applying these principles directly at my internship at SOMA Foundation Rwanda. We maintain an offline educational web application that runs on resource-constrained offline mini PCs in rural schools. Previously, fetching static pages, digital books, and multimedia was experiencing noticeable latency. Applying the caching patterns, query optimizations, and lightweight data structures learned in this course made content delivery significantly smoother and faster on limited hardware. Moving forward, I will continue applying these lessons to all my software projects—ensuring clean RESTful API contracts, defensive concurrency modeling, database-level constraint enforcement, and resilient asynchronous queue processing.
